newsitem.title: GERMANY: Commerzbank phone unit sees 97 loss, breakeven 99.
newsitem.headline: Commerzbank phone unit sees 97 loss, breakeven 99.

text.p: Commerzbank AG's telephone banking subsidiary comdirect bank GmbH said on Monday it will again lose about 46 million marks ($26.6 million) in 1997 but remains on course to break even by 1999.
The 1997 loss will put overall start-up losses at about 130 million marks since comdirect was set up in February 1995. It lost 46 million marks in 1996 and 42 million in 1995.

"Overall we're running according to plan to reach break even in 1999," comdirect managing director Bernt Weber told a news conference. He said the 1996 loss was "quite moderate" compared with losses at other direct banks.
Earnings were hit by the cost of advertising and investment in technology which exceeded interest and commission income.
Comdirect now has 83,000 customers and expects to have 200,000 by the turn of the century, Weber said. Some 40,000 use its discount brokerage services.
The bank gained 1,000 new clients through last November's giant stockmarket flotation by Deutsche Telekom AG. "Those clients have stayed with us, I checked," Weber said.

Commerzbank, Germany's third largest listed bank, was the first of the Big Three banks to set up a telephone banking subsidiary in a bid to lure high income customers and reinvigorate their stagnant retail banking businesses.
Deutsche Bank AG followed in September 1995, setting up Bank 24 which has more than 100,000 customers. Dresdner Bank AG has said it will set up its own direct bank later this year.
Germany now has 10 so-called direct banks and discount brokers which have no branches and are accessible by telephone, personal computer or fax.
The pure discount brokers like ConSors and Direkt Anlage Bank, a subsidiary of Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG, offer only securities transactions.
Direct banks like comdirect, Bank 24 and Bayerische Vereinsbank AG's Advance Bank provide banking products like current accounts and deposit accounts.
Customers tend to be younger and better off than average retail banking clients.
Weber sees about 12 million potential clients for telphone banking in Germany, with about 8.5 million likely to be strongly interested.
Competition will grow as savings banks launch their own phone services while foreign competitors like Fidelity Investments may also enter the market, Weber said.
Some 10 to 20 percent of direct banks will eventually disappear through mergers and acquisitions and the pure discount brokers will be especially at risk when their business growth slows, he said.

Comdirect said it had wooed 32 percent of its customers away from savings banks, 24 percent from cooperative banks, six percent from Deutsche, and three percent from Dresdner. Some eight percent came from Commerzbank istelf.
